description: The challenge is to develop an intelligent health-monitoring application for astronauts during space missions. By using real NASA health data, data visualization, and artificial intelligence, the platform aims to track physiological indicators, analyze health trends, detect unusual changes, and provide science-based insights to support astronauts' well-being and safety in space.
summary: SILA is a health monitoring prototype for astronauts on missions far from Earth, where a ground doctor may not be able to respond in time. It collects vital signs (simulated in the prototype), shows them on a personal astronaut dashboard and a crew overview for the ground doctor, and raises color-coded alerts with a transparent rules engine, never with AI. An AI assistant explains alerts in plain language, never gives a diagnosis, receives only anonymized data, and falls back to predefined answers if it is unavailable. For an astronaut under high stress, an emergency mode lets them press a button or say a trigger phrase, describe the situation by voice or text, and send it straight to the doctor, who sees it in real time. The monitored parameters follow NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight and its risk areas.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SILA monitors the health of astronauts during long missions. Astronauts get a personal dashboard (latest values, trend charts, status cards, recommendations, an AI chat and an emergency button). The ground doctor gets a crew overview, active alerts, a filterable history, an AI-generated crew summary and real-time emergency reports.

HOW IT WORKS

A Node.js simulator sends measurements to an Express API. A deterministic rules engine compares each value with thresholds (attention and critical levels, personal thresholds supported, duplicate alerts avoided) and stores measurements and alerts in MySQL/MariaDB. Socket.IO pushes new data, alerts and emergency reports to the Angular dashboards in real time. Alerts never depend on AI. A server-side AI assistant explains alerts and summarizes the crew in plain language; it never gives a diagnosis, receives only anonymized data, shows a permanent warning, and switches to a backup mode with predefined answers when the AI service is unavailable.

Emergency mode: an astronaut under stress presses a red button or says "emergency", "mayday" or "code red". A simple high-contrast screen opens, the astronaut describes the situation by voice (transcribed) or text, and the report is sent to the ground doctor automatically after a few seconds of silence. A cancel button prevents false alarms.

BENEFITS AND GOAL

Earlier recognition of abnormal readings, a clear next step for the astronaut, and an easier route to the medical team when stress makes ordinary navigation difficult. The design is built around NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, especially distance from Earth and behavioral stress.

TOOLS

Angular (TypeScript), Chart.js, RxJS, Node.js, Express, Socket.IO, MySQL/MariaDB, a large language model API, the browser Web Speech API, Figma, Git and GitHub.

LIMITATIONS

All measurements are simulated. Alert thresholds are indicative values chosen by the team, not NASA values, and need medical validation. SILA is not a medical device. Speech recognition currently needs an Internet connection (Chrome or Edge). Offline synchronization, onboard AI and real sensors are future work.

NASA RESOURCES USED

We used three NASA Human Research Program resources as the scientific basis of the design (links listed in the NASA Data field). No NASA dataset was imported: measurements are simulated and our alert thresholds are indicative values chosen by the team, not NASA values.

- 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight: the five hazards and the point that they can worsen each other. Distance from Earth led to alerts that work without AI and without ground guidance; an astronaut's status takes the most severe color among all parameters.

- Risks of Human Spaceflight: Risk of Hypoxia -> blood oxygen (SpO2); Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules -> sleep duration; Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations -> heart rate and blood pressure; Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders -> emergency mode; Risk of Inadequate Systems Operations Support -> AI assistant with a backup mode.

- Ongoing HRP Research in Space: Artemis II studies ARCHeR (activity and sleep) and Standard Measures (a consistent set of measurements for every crew member) inspired timestamped measurements and the same parameters for every astronaut.
